scams.name: Scopolamine Drink Spiking (Devil's Breath)
scams.description:
You match with an attractive woman on Tinder in Cali and agree to meet at a bar in Granada. She is charming, the conversation flows, and she insists on ordering a round of aguardiente. You excuse yourself to the bathroom. When you return and finish your drink, your memory goes blank. You wake up in your hotel room 14 hours later with no phone, no wallet, no watch, and your bank accounts drained. You have no memory of anything after that drink.

Scopolamine — known locally as burundanga or 'devil's breath' — is extracted from the Brugmansia plant that grows wild throughout the Andes. In January 2024 the US Embassy issued a warning about dating-app attacks in Colombia after eight US citizens died in suspicious circumstances in Medellín in late 2023; Colombian authorities reported 39 tourist deaths in Medellín across 2024, roughly half of them American. While most press coverage focused on Medellín, Cali — Colombia's third-largest city — hosts the same criminal networks using the same methods. The drug renders victims completely compliant or unconscious for up to 24 hours. Travel-safety guides describe the typical playbook: attractive women target male visitors who appear wealthy at bars or on dating sites and slip scopolamine into their drinks when the mark goes to the bathroom. In February 2024 Match Group, the parent company of Tinder and Hinge, dispatched representatives to Colombia to meet with authorities after the crisis escalated; Colombian police have since arrested multiple women accused of drugging and robbing tourists in coordinated gang operations.
scams.avoidance: Never leave your drink unattended — take it with you to the bathroom or order a fresh one when you return Meet dating app matches only in busy public places and tell a friend or hotel reception your plans with the person's details Do not accept drinks from strangers, food samples from street vendors, or cigarettes from anyone you do not know Watch your drink being prepared and served — scopolamine can be slipped into drinks, applied to paper, or even blown in your face in powdered form If you suddenly feel very dizzy or disoriented, immediately tell the bartender or bouncer — do not wait or try to walk home alone
scams.location: Salsa clubs in Juanchito, bars in Menga and Granada neighborhoods, Parque del Perro area, and dating app meetups

scams.name: The Motorcycle Phone Snatch
scams.description:
You are walking through Cali's San Antonio neighborhood, checking your phone for directions. A motorcycle with two riders slows beside you. In a fraction of a second, the passenger reaches out and rips the phone from your hand. The motorcycle accelerates and disappears into traffic. You are left standing on the sidewalk, unable to even get a plate number.

Motorcycle-based phone snatching is one of Cali's most common street crimes. The pattern is consistent: a moto pulls alongside a pedestrian in a fashionable barrio like Granada and the passenger tears a phone, gold necklace, or camera strap free before accelerating away. The UK Foreign Office travel advisory for Colombia flags 'mugging by people on motorcycles' as a specific warning. Colombia's national 'No dar papaya' principle — literally 'don't give papaya,' meaning don't make yourself an easy target — exists because of how common this kind of opportunistic theft is. The national government has deployed an additional thousand police to Cali and overall theft is trending downward, but phone snatching remains an everyday occurrence. Gold chains, watches, bags, and cameras are all targets for the motorcycle grab-and-run.
scams.avoidance: Never use your phone while walking near any road in Cali — step inside a shop, cafe, or doorway if you need to check your phone Walk on the side of the sidewalk furthest from the street, keeping buildings between you and traffic Keep your phone in a front zippered pocket, not in your hand, and use earbuds for navigation so you do not need to look at the screen Do not wear visible gold chains, expensive watches, or flashy jewelry in any part of Cali If you must carry your phone visible, use a phone lanyard clipped to your belt or bag strap so it cannot be snatched cleanly
scams.location: Major intersections throughout Cali, especially along Avenida Sexta, Avenida Roosevelt, near Parque del Perro, and the San Antonio neighborhood

scams.name: Salsa Club Pickpocketing
scams.description:
You head to Juanchito — Cali's legendary salsa strip — for a night of dancing. The clubs are packed, the music is incredible, and a local woman invites you to dance. While you are focused on the steps and the close contact, her companion lifts your wallet from your back pocket. Alternatively, your phone disappears from the table while you are on the dance floor. You do not notice until you try to pay for drinks and realize your wallet is gone.

Cali is the undisputed salsa capital of the world, and its clubs are a major tourist draw — which makes them a prime target for pickpockets. Travel-safety guides consistently flag crowded salsa clubs as the likeliest place a visitor to Cali will experience petty theft. The close physical contact inherent in salsa — hands on waists, proximity, spinning — creates ideal conditions for skilled pickpockets. Juanchito's clubs are particularly packed Thursday through Saturday, with dance floors where it is impossible to maintain awareness of every pocket and belonging. The problem is not limited to professional criminals — opportunistic theft by other clubgoers is also common when valuables are left on tables.
scams.avoidance: Leave your wallet, passport, and cards at the hotel — bring only enough cash for the night in a front pocket Use a slim money belt or neck wallet under your shirt for your cash and phone Never leave your phone, camera, or bag unattended on a table — keep them on your body or leave them at the hotel Go to salsa clubs with a group rather than alone — one person can always watch the table and belongings Choose reputable clubs with coat check or locker services (like Tin Tin Deo) where you can secure valuables before dancing
scams.location: Salsa clubs in Juanchito, Tin Tin Deo, La Topa Tolondra, Zaperoco, and Menga nightlife district

scams.name: Fake Police ID Shakedown
scams.description:
You are walking back to your hostel in San Antonio when two men in plain clothes step out from a side street. One flashes a badge and says he is a police officer. He claims there is a drug problem in the area and he needs to inspect your wallet and bag. His partner stands behind you. He takes your wallet to 'check for counterfeit bills,' palming several hundred thousand pesos in the process. He hands it back, tells you everything is fine, and they disappear.

The fake police scam is one of the most dangerous cons in Colombia. The standard variant has a corrupt or impersonated officer either stealing bills from a foreigner's wallet or planting drugs and then demanding a hefty bribe to make the matter disappear. The encounter typically happens on the street, in transit hubs, or around bars at night: criminals stop a traveler, flash an ID or badge quickly, and ask to inspect documents or cash. A newer variant is the fake multa — scammers impersonating officers who issue 'fines' that must be paid on the spot in cash. The single fact a tourist should anchor on: real Colombian police will never ask to inspect your cash, check for counterfeit bills on the street, or demand an on-the-spot payment of any kind.
scams.avoidance: Never hand over your wallet, cash, or passport to anyone on the street — offer to walk to the nearest police station instead Carry only a photocopy of your passport (the data page and entry stamp) — leave the original at the hotel safe If confronted, say loudly 'Vamos a la estación de policía' (Let's go to the police station) — scammers will back off Real Colombian police carry a standardized ID card with a photo, rank, and badge number — ask to see it and photograph it Walk toward a crowded area, enter a shop, or flag down a passing taxi if the interaction feels threatening
scams.location: Streets near Parque del Perro, Barrio San Antonio, areas outside hostels and tourist accommodations, quiet streets at night

scams.name: The Millionaire's Taxi Ride (Express Kidnapping)
scams.description:
After a night out in Menga, you hail a taxi on the street. Ten minutes into the ride, the driver picks up another passenger — his accomplice. They drive to a series of ATMs, holding you for hours as you are forced to withdraw the daily maximum at each machine. This is called the 'paseo millonario' — the millionaire's ride — and it is one of Colombia's most documented crimes against tourists.

The 'millionaire's ride' script is simple and widely reported: a traveler hails a street taxi that turns out to be unlicensed; instead of going to the stated destination the driver turns down a backstreet where his accomplices — often armed with knives — are waiting. Victims have been held in taxis for over three hours while assailants drained their bank accounts and made fraudulent online purchases. In documented cases, amounts like two million pesos (roughly \$458) are transferred electronically alongside stolen phones, watches, wallets, and jewelry. The UK Foreign Office, the Canadian government, and the US State Department all warn about express kidnappings via street-hailed taxis in Colombian cities. The practical rule for Cali: never hail a taxi from the street, especially at night.
scams.avoidance: NEVER hail a taxi from the street in Cali — use InDrive, Uber, or DiDi exclusively, where rides are tracked and drivers are identified If ride-hailing apps are unavailable, have your hotel or restaurant call a registered taxi company for you Share your live location with a friend or family member before getting into any vehicle Set low daily ATM withdrawal limits through your banking app — this limits what criminals can extract even in a worst-case scenario Keep most of your cash, cards, and your passport in the hotel safe — carry only what you need for the outing
scams.location: Street-hailed taxis throughout Cali, especially outside nightlife districts, at night, and near bus terminals

scams.name: Nightclub Drink Overcharging Scam
scams.description:
You open a tab at a bar near Parque del Perro, ordering beers and aguardiente shots for yourself and new friends you have made. The night is great and you are having a blast. When you close your tab, the bill shows 25 drinks instead of the 12 you ordered. The bartender insists the count is correct and points to tally marks on a napkin that you cannot verify. If you argue, a bouncer materializes. You pay the 450,000 COP bill (roughly \$110 USD) rather than cause a scene.

Bar tab inflation is a known tactic in Colombian nightlife, particularly at venues catering to tourists. Scam guides covering patterns common across Colombian cities warn about bars that add phantom drinks to tabs, charge for drinks you bought others that were never delivered, or run inflated prices for foreigners. Tourist-targeted venues often operate in partnership with touts who bring in foreigners and then overcharge them. In some cases, bar staff will 'ring the bell' — a tradition where if you hit the bar bell, you buy everyone a round — and then add it to your bill when you never actually rang it.
scams.avoidance: Pay for each round as you go rather than running a tab — this makes it impossible to add phantom drinks Ask the price of drinks before ordering and keep a running count on your phone's notes app Do not ring any bells, accept unsolicited drinks, or agree to buy rounds for groups of people you just met Stick to established, well-reviewed bars and clubs rather than places suggested by strangers If the bill seems wrong, calmly ask for an itemized breakdown and dispute specific charges — most bars will adjust rather than lose the tourist
scams.location: Bars and clubs in Menga, La Sexta, Parque del Perro area, and Juanchito strip
